items.note: Claim A asserts that there is no difference in psychological well-being between non-users and low users, whereas Claim B asserts that light users have higher psychological well-being than non-users.
Claim A asserts that depression rates increased in post-World War II birth cohorts, whereas Claim B finds no birth-year effect on depression rates for cohorts born between 1965 and 1996.

Claim A states that evidence regarding the link between cyberbullying and suicidality is conflicting, whereas Claim B asserts a clear and strong association between cyberbullying victimization and suicidal ideation.

Claim A suggests that smartphone adoption meaningfully contributes to a decline in adolescent well-being, whereas Claim B asserts that the link between digital technology use and well-being is too small to be practically significant.

Claim A asserts that social media use predicts declines in life satisfaction over time, whereas Claim B finds that the longitudinal within-person effect of social media use on life satisfaction is trivial in size.

Claim A asserts that historical changes in depression rates reflect real cohort shifts rather than measurement artifacts, whereas Claim B finds no evidence of increased depression prevalence when controlling for recall artifacts through concurrent assessment.
